title: Files, Classes, Charts
summary: Read and write files with open() and with, and split a CSV line by hand. Bundle data and methods with class Position, and save line, bar and histogram charts to PNG files with matplotlib. These starters come without finished versions, so shell commands are used to check the expected results ahead of time.

journal_by_hand.summary: Practice 1. Open the trades.csv next to the program with open(), skip the one header line, split each remaining line into fields with strip() and split(","), and count whether the action (fields[2]) is buy or sell. It is an exercise in doing by hand what pd.read_csv does.
journal_by_hand.notes: With nano journal_by_hand.py, write a for line in f: loop where the TODO is, increase the two counters, and at the end print print("buy", buys) and print("sell", sells). Run it again and compare with the shell result above.
steps: The first line holds the column names date,ticker,action,shares,price, and below it comes one trade per line. 11 lines in total = 1 header line + 10 trades.
The starter opens the file, reads only the header and closes it. There is no output and exit=0. When the with block ends, the file is closed automatically.

repr shows that the header returned by readline() ends with \n. Removing it with strip() and cutting with split(",") gives a list of five strings. Even the numbers are strings like '10', so they must be converted with int() before they can be multiplied: TEA buy 50000.
Splitting without strip() leaves the last field as '5000\n', which is not equal to "5000" (False). This is the trap where the newline at the end of the line ruins a comparison.
Count the third column (action) with shell tools to see the answer ahead of time: buy 6, sell 4 (the 1 action is the header). The finished program should print two lines, buy 6 and sell 4.

position_report.summary: Practice 2. The Position class stores ticker, shares and buy on self in __init__. Add a profit(self, close) method, build Position objects from the five rows, and print each stock's profit or loss on the screen while writing the same lines to portfolio_report.txt.
position_report.notes: The TypeError in the last step is an intended error reproducing the TRAP from the slides. The finished program should print CODE +8000, TEA -8000, ROBO +25000, MLBK +15000, FIT +24000 and Saved portfolio_report.txt; check with cat portfolio_report.txt that the same five lines were saved to the file. To get the report onto your computer, run cp portfolio_report.txt /mnt/host/ and then enter its name in the Download box.
steps: The starter only defines the class and the data, so there is no output, and the report file has not been created yet (No such file or directory).
Two objects made from one class each have their own attributes: CODE 10, then CODE 2 10000. Importing a module runs its top-level code, but this starter has no print, so it stays quiet.
There is no profit method yet, so this is False. Once you add the method it becomes True, and Position("TEA", 40, 5000).profit(4800) should return -8000.
Calling a method whose def leaves out self gives TypeError: P.profit() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given. This is because Python passes the object itself as the first argument in the call.

my_charts.summary: Lab 1. Save CODE's week of closing prices as a line chart with markers, a title, a y-axis label and a grid to week.png, then start a new figure with plt.figure() and save the five stocks' values as a bar chart to values.png.
my_charts.notes: What to check when you are done: week.png has a single line joining five points, with a title and a grid, and values.png has five bars with a title and a y axis in won. The two charts must not overlap in one file. The y axis starts near 9800, not 0 (matplotlib fits it to the data range).
steps: The starter imports matplotlib and only builds lists. There is no output and no PNG file (ls reports No such file or directory). On the first run you may see the notice Matplotlib is building the font cache once. This virtual machine has no screen, so you must create files with plt.savefig() instead of plt.show().
Saves the line chart and bar chart from the slides separately. Without the plt.figure() between the two charts, the bars would be drawn on top of the line in a single file.
Two PNGs were created. After copying them to /mnt/host/, enter demo_line.png in the page's Download box to save it to your computer and open it.
Deletes the practice files. The finished my_charts.py should print High: 10800, Saved week.png, Saved values.png.

year_report.summary: Lab 2. Read a file of closing prices for the 260 trading days of 2026 with pd.read_csv, save CODE's year as a line chart (code_year.png) and the daily changes diff().dropna() as a histogram (changes.png), and print the number of trading days, the best close and its date.
year_report.notes: The finished program should print Days: 260, Best close: 12795, Best date: 2026-08-06, Saved code_year.png, Saved changes.png. The histogram has 259 changes, one fewer, because the first day has no previous day. Download the charts with cp code_year.png changes.png /mnt/host/ followed by the Download box.
steps: The columns are date and five stocks (CODE, TEA, ROBO, MLBK, FIT). 261 lines = 1 header line + 260 trading days.
The starter only reads the CSV and takes out the CODE column. Loading pandas takes a while, and there is no output. If the file were missing, a FileNotFoundError would have occurred here.
In the shell, the last line after sorting by the second column (CODE) is the best close: 12795 on 2026-08-06. It is the same value the finished program should find with idxmax().
March 2–6 is the week from the earlier pandas story. The CODE column, 10000, 10200, 9800, 10500, 10800, matches the earlier pandas examples.

journal_chart.summary: Lab 3 (take-home). Read the trade journal with pd.read_csv, draw the buy/sell counts from value_counts as a bar chart (journal.png), and print the two counts and the total amount traded (the sum of shares * price).
steps: The starter only reads the CSV into a DataFrame and prints nothing. read_csv does for every line the strip, split and int() you did by hand in Practice 1.
Skipping the header in the shell and adding up shares × price gives Traded: 340000. The finished program should print buy 6, sell 4, Traded: 340000, Saved journal.png.

make_prices_2026.summary: The generator script that created prices_2026.csv. random.seed(2026) makes it use the same random sequence every time, so each run produces a file that is identical down to the byte. The week of March 2–6 is pinned to the closing prices from the earlier pandas examples.
steps: prices_2026.csv: 260 trading days, 5 tickers. Counting only the weekdays (Mon–Fri) of 2026 gives 260 days.
The newly made file and the copy in the starter folder do not differ by a single byte (identical). With the same seed, random gives the same results.
The portfolio.csv in the same folder is the table from the my_portfolio.py you wrote earlier, saved as CSV. Each stock's close equals its March 6 close in prices_2026.csv.
